sections.category: Agent-security funding and a working Claude Cowork sandbox escape land in the same week, hardening the case that the AI-agent runtime is now its own attack surface with a dedicated defensive market forming around it

bullets.body: Straiker, a startup that pitches itself as the agentic-security company, closed a $64 million Series A led by Marathon Management Partners with Citi Ventures, Illuminate Financial, and Workday Ventures, taking its total raised to $85 million, per SiliconANGLE. Its platform is built around three products, Discover AI for finding agents and their tool access across an enterprise, Ascend AI for pre-deployment adversarial red-teaming, and Defend AI for runtime guardrails that watch behavior and stop threats in real time, and the company says run-rate revenue grew more than 15x in under a year, according to Straiker's own announcement. The funding lands the same week a concrete failure mode went public: researchers at Armadin detailed a full sandbox-escape chain in Anthropic's Claude Cowork that lets an attacker with local code execution reach root inside the isolated Ubuntu VM by abusing a resume flag that skips unprivileged-user creation and a domain-override parameter that disables the network allowlist, per SiliconANGLE and Cybersecurity News. Anthropic shipped a patch on June 30 that hardens namespace boundaries, tightens seccomp profiles, and drops extra Linux capabilities, while disputing that it qualified as a security issue because exploitation presumes existing host access. The through-line is that the agent runtime, the sandbox that is supposed to contain what an autonomous agent does, is now both a live vulnerability class and a funded product category rather than a theoretical concern.

sections.category: Raja Koduri's Oxmiq raises $35M to license an AI GPU architecture rather than sell chips, and pulls Jim Keller onto its board, opening a new front where custom-silicon design itself becomes the product

bullets.body: Oxmiq Labs, founded by former Intel and AMD graphics chief Raja Koduri, closed a $35 million Series A that brings its total to $60 million, led by backers including the Samsung Catalyst Fund and Fundomo with participation from MediaTek, Pegatron Venture Capital, and others, per SiliconANGLE. Rather than fabricating and selling accelerators, Oxmiq is commercializing OxCore, a licensable GPU architecture that folds the graphics, CPU, and tensor-accelerator roles usually split across separate blocks into a single design a chipmaker can build a custom AI processor on without running a full ground-up chip program, according to the company's release. Koduri frames the ambition explicitly as becoming the Arm of the AI-silicon era, licensing the foundation instead of competing SKU-for-SKU with NVIDIA and AMD. The signal that this is more than a slide deck is the board addition of Jim Keller, the Tenstorrent CEO whose name is attached to some of the industry's most consequential architectures, per The Next Web. For buyers watching the non-NVIDIA field, the interesting shift is that the competitive layer is moving upstream from finished parts to the IP that lets any system builder spin its own, which is a structurally different way to attack the accelerator incumbency than yet another standalone inference ASIC.

sections.category: Unsloth ships DeepSeek-V4 fine-tuning support the same week the model graduates from preview, closing the gap between a 1.6T open-weight frontier release and the consumer-GPU tuning stack that can adapt it

bullets.body: Unsloth added DeepSeek-V4 support with all reasoning levels enabled in its Studio build tagged July 7, 2026, per the Unsloth changelog, extending the fine-tuning stack to the largest open-weight family it now covers alongside GLM-5.2 and MiniMax-M3. The timing tracks DeepSeek-V4's own trajectory: the Pro and Flash variants, a 1.6-trillion-parameter MoE with roughly 49 billion active parameters and a one-million-token context and its 284-billion-parameter sibling, first shipped in April as an MIT-licensed preview and are now moving to an official mid-July release with refined pricing, per MindStudio and DeepSeek's API documentation. The reason this pairing matters is that an open-weight model at that scale is only practically useful to most teams if a tuning path exists that does not require a full training cluster, and Unsloth's whole pitch is cutting the VRAM and time cost of adapting these models on commodity hardware. With the serving side also converging, DeepSeek-V4 has publicly endorsed SGLang and vLLM for inference, the practical read for anyone building on open weights is that the download-tune-serve loop for a genuine frontier-tier Chinese model is now a same-week, off-the-shelf pipeline rather than a bespoke engineering project.

sections.category: OpenAI pushes lower-latency voice into general use with gpt-realtime-2.1 and lines up a three-tier GPT-5.6 lineup, steering the frontier toward cheaper voice-agent and enterprise deployment economics

bullets.body: OpenAI released gpt-realtime-2.1 and a smaller gpt-realtime-2.1-mini on July 6, 2026, advertising at least 25 percent lower p95 latency across its realtime voice models along with better alphanumeric recognition, silence and noise handling, and interruption behavior, with the mini tier priced well below the full model to widen access for speech-to-speech agents, per OpenAI's release notes. In parallel, OpenAI opened a limited preview of GPT-5.6 to a small set of trusted partners, a three-model family named Sol, Terra, and Luna with published per-million-token pricing of $5/$30, $2.50/$15, and $1/$6 respectively and a broader rollout promised in the coming weeks, according to the same notes and reporting collected by LLM-Stats. The pattern across both moves is a deliberate push down the cost curve and toward operational deployment rather than raw capability headlines: a tiered lineup that lets builders pick a cheaper Luna or Terra tier for high-volume work, and a realtime update explicitly tuned for the voice-agent workflows enterprises are trying to ship. For teams weighing hosted frontier APIs against self-hosted open weights, the read is that the closed-model side is competing increasingly on latency and price-per-tier, exactly the axes on which the open-weight serving stacks have been making their own case.

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: ICML runs all week in Seoul and an AI Tinkerers SF meetup lands tomorrow, while UN AI-governance talks converge on Geneva and the chip, security, and enterprise tracks stack up through the fall

bullets.body: The live item for research this week is ICML 2026 in Seoul, with the main conference running July 7-9 and workshops July 10-11 at the COEX center. For Bay Area locals, AI Tinkerers San Francisco hosts its next meetup July 8, a go-to-market engineering track in the usual three-hour working-demo format. On the governance side, the UN's first Global Dialogue on AI Governance is convening all 193 member states in Geneva on July 6-7 at Palexpo, alongside the ITU AI for Good summit, with the new Independent International Scientific Panel on AI presenting a preliminary report, useful context for anyone tracking agent-safety and cyber-misuse rulemaking. On the AI-chip and hardware track, AMD's MI400 Instinct series and Helios rack-scale system remain the marquee second-half-2026 catalyst, while the nearest confirmed hardware gathering is Hot Chips 2026 at Stanford's Memorial Auditorium on August 23-25 (early registration closes July 31), followed by the AI Infra Summit in Santa Clara on September 15-17. The AI-security block clusters in early-to-mid August: SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is August 11-12 at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay, Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village land in Las Vegas in early August, and OWASP Global AppSec USA follows in San Francisco on November 5-6; Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series continues its stops for teams focused on agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense. On the enterprise track, Ai4 2026 runs August 4-6 at The Venetian in Las Vegas, the ACM AI Leadership Summit is August 30 to September 2 in Atlanta, GitHub Universe is October 28-29, and AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas. The two immediate actions are catching the ICML program through July 11 if research is your beat and the July 8 AI Tinkerers SF meetup if you are local; the August AI Risk Summit and Hot Chips remain the natural next venues for confidential-inference and secure-accelerator announcements.
